question: Tom Vandendriessche is a member of the Flemish opposition party, Vlaams Belang, which, according to polls, is the largest party in both Flanders and Belgium. His Facebook page has 235 000 followers and he had a reach of 150 000 people by mail. Tom Vandendriessche still reaches some 3000 people on Facebook.

The issue here is the shadowbanning that has been going on for some time, and which prevents him from communicating adequately with his constituents. The fact that a foreign company can exert such influence over European elections should be of great concern to us. With this practice of shadowbanning, Facebook is curtailing free speech, freedom of information and the need for fair elections in a democratic society.
The following questions thus arise: 1.
Is the Commission aware of shadowbanning practices targetting politicians on social media platforms?
Does the Commission consider that such practices constitute unauthorised foreign interference in the democratic process?
How does the Commission intend to stop and prevent such heavy-handed foreign interference?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.6.2024) Regulation 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act – ‘DSA’)1 mentions (Recital 55) shadow banning as a restriction of visibility that consists in demotion in ranking or in recommender systems, as well as in limiting accessibility by one or more recipients of the service or blocking the user from an online community without the user being aware2.

The Commission has taken action within its supervisory powers under the DSA to investigate compliance with the DSA by a number of providers of very large online platforms (VLOPs), including in relation to shadow banning.

On 30 April 2024, the Commission opened formal proceedings against Meta, including in relation to the policy linked to the ‘political content approach’, that demotes political content in the recommender systems3.

The opening of proceedings is based on a preliminary analysis of Meta’s risk assessment report, replies to the Commission’s formal requests for information (RFIs), publicly available reports and the Commission’s own analysis. An overview of the designated VLOPs and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) supervised by the Commission and the main enforcement activities is available on the Commission’s website4.

If at the end of an investigation, it is found that a provider has not complied, it can face a fine of up to 6% of its worldwide turnover. Additionally, the Commission has published guidelines for providers of very large platforms, including for Meta’s services on the mitigation of systemic risks for electoral processes5.

The guidelines recommend mitigation measures and best practices including reinforcing internal processes, adopting specific mitigation measures linked to generative artificial intelligence and specific recommendations for the upcoming European Parliament elections.
